title: 2025-04-15-tool-calling-json-mode-deep-dive
summary: Deep dive on JSON-mode / constrained decoding and tool/function calling performance. Covered tradeoffs in latency and throughput, KV-cache interactions, batching strategies, and quantization impacts for on-prem/VPC deployments. Agreed to run a benchmark with Atlas sample workload and share config + security docs.
topics: KV cache interactions with structured outputs
Quantization impact on generation quality and KV cache
On-prem / VPC considerations for latency and throughput
transcript:
HEADER
Date: 2025-04-15T15:00:00Z
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Atlas ML), Carlos Ortega (Atlas Infra), Lina Park (Atlas CTO)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining. want to run through the deep dive on JSON mode and our function calling behavior, especially how it affects latency and throughput in Dedicated and Private setups. Diego will lead most of the perf stuff.
[00:18] Diego: hi all, quick agenda: constrained decoding mechanics, how we implement tool-calling, batching + KV cache interactions, quantization notes, then Q/A and next steps.
[00:30] Maya: sounds good, our main pain is we need guaranteed valid JSON responses for downstream parsers, and low tail latency for 99th pct. throughput is important too because we do bursts.
[00:42] Lina: and security/regulatory: anything that affects audit logs or KMS usage we need to know.
[00:50] Diego: noted. quick context: Atlas uses a sync endpoint currently through a proxy in their VPC, runs ~120 rps baseline with spikes to 800 rps, typical prompt size ~80 tokens, responses ~120 tokens JSON object with nested fields, and they call an internal billing service via function call for enrichment.
[01:12] Carlos: correct; also we have strict egress policies so Private/VPC is likely.
[01:20] Diego: ok, constrained decoding (JSON-mode) overview: basically we run a token-level state machine that enforces grammar constraints so the model only emits valid JSON tokens. That adds CPU overhead on the generation side because every candidate token needs to be validated against the automaton. On GPU-first runtimes this can create a host-device roundtrip unless we push the automaton logic into a GPU-friendly kernel.
[01:45] Maya: is there a big difference between your hosted versus Dedicated/Private?
[01:50] Diego: the core difference is how much of that validation we can batch and whether we can execute the constraint checks on-device. In Redwood hosted we currently offload some checks to a batched CPU path optimized in our runtime; for Dedicated/Private deployments we can enable a GPU-constrained decoder that minimizes roundtrips, but that depends on driver/kernel support and quantization format.
[02:15] Avery: in practice that means JSON-mode adds X-20 to X+50 ms depending on sequence length and model, right? can you give a ballpark?
[02:22] Diego: ballpark: for a 120-token response with typical model (open 7B-ish), we see additional ~8-30 ms per request when using our optimized GPU path; if constrained decoding is done on CPU per token the penalty can be 40-120 ms. For larger models latencies change but relative overhead reduces because compute dominates.
[02:45] Maya: hmm, our 99th pct tail currently is around 220ms and we need <=300ms. Sounds close.
[02:52] Diego: right, and batching changes that: if you batch many requests, amortized overhead for constraint checks drops, but batching increases per-request latency due to queueing. So it's a throughput vs single-request-latency tradeoff.
[03:10] Carlos: how does KV cache factor in? We have many repeated prefixes across requests.
[03:18] Diego: KV cache is great: for prefix reuse it reduces compute significantly. But with constrained decoding there are some edge cases: if you cache encodings for a prefix but the constrained decoder state also depends on partial parse state (e.g., open arrays, expected schema), you need to cache decoder automaton state alongside KV cache. Redwood runtime supports storing a compact constraint-state fingerprint with each cache entry to avoid re-evaluating the grammar from scratch.
[03:46] Maya: is that fingerprint compatible with quantized models? we plan to run int8 quantized weights to save memory.
[03:52] Diego: yes, mostly. Quantization affects model logits behavior a bit; the constraint-state fingerprint is independent of numeric format because it's about structural parse, but when using int8 kernels you sometimes see slightly different token probabilities which can change beam-like searches. For deterministic constrained decoding (no sampling), quantization is less of an issue.
[04:16] Lina: you mentioned beam-like. we usually use greedy decoding with constraints. any specific impact?
[04:22] Diego: greedy constrained decoding is the simplest: at each step we pick the highest-prob token that satisfies grammar. So the overhead is just checking candidates. With beam search you multiply checks by beam-size. For JSON-mode with strict schema enforcement we recommend greedy/deterministic decoders to keep CPU costs predictable.
[04:42] Maya: ok. on the tool-calling side: how are function calls executed? do you serialize the call and wait inside the model or do you return a special token?
[04:52] Diego: two patterns: synchronous function-call inside generation (model emits a CALL token and we pause generation while external tool executes, then resume with return content) or we do offline post-hoc extraction where the model returns a structured payload and the runtime triggers the tool. Synchronous calls are easier for single-turn workflows but introduce blocking I/O during generation which can hurt throughput unless you have a non-blocking runtime that can context-switch.
[05:18] Carlos: so synchronous would block that GPU slot?
[05:22] Diego: depends on runtime: our runtime supports releasing the GPU while waiting if the tool is external and the call is IO-bound, but that requires the runtime to checkpoint KV cache and context, and potentially re-load - we have an internal fast-swap mechanism but it adds complexity. For Dedicated/Private deployments we can configure policies: either reserve the worker for the full duration or swap out and requeue.
[05:44] Maya: interesting. what about batching when some requests need tool calls and others dont?
[05:50] Diego: mixed batches are harder. If a batch contains a request that needs a synchronous external call, the batch can stall. Our scheduler tries to avoid mixing interactive tool-call requests with pure generation by routing them to different pools or using quick rejection/bypass flags. For Atlas workload, we can keep a small pool of compute nodes dedicated to tool-calls.
[06:12] Avery: can you run through an example latency budget for Atlas: 120 rps baseline, 20% tool-calling enrichments, 120 token output, constrained JSON.
[06:21] Diego: quick back-of-envelope: if pure generation path avg latency is 70ms (GPU optimized, batched little), JSON constrained extra 15ms, so 85ms. For 20% tool calls with synchronous blocking and a 50ms tool latency, if we reserve worker the request is ~135ms; if we offload and requeue maybe 85ms + scheduling overhead (30-60ms) so similar. Tail gets worse if tool latency spikes. So overall 99th pct could approach your 300ms SLO depending on spikes.
[07:02] Maya: can you quantify throughput in tokens/sec for your recommended Dedicated config?
[07:08] Diego: with our Dedicated A100 pool, for 7B model and int8 quant we see sustained per-GPU throughput roughly 150-250k tokens/sec depending on batch shape and kv cache hit rate. With KV cache hits for prefixes you can effectively increase request throughput because decoding steps per request drop.
[07:34] Carlos: our infra team worries about memory: KV cache per session grows with sequence length and concurrent sessions. Any heuristics?
[07:42] Diego: yes, common heuristics: TTL-based eviction, LRU on per-customer prefix frequency, and per-route cache max size. Also store compressed KV entries for quantized models; for int8 we store keys/values in 16-bit compressed format in our implementation to save memory. We can provide recommended config based on your 800 rps burst pattern.
[08:04] Lina: what about reliability and fallbacks? if constrained decoder fails to produce valid JSON due to model mistake, what's the recovery?
[08:12] Diego: our runtime can detect impossible states and trigger fallbacks: either re-run decoding with relaxed constraints or switch to a parser-based repair loop: generate free-text then run a separate validator/parser model to patch. There's also an option to fallback to a smaller deterministically-trained schema model for post-processing. All of these are config flags per route.
[08:36] Maya: do you have any benchmark docs we can run against?
[08:40] Avery: yes we have a bench spreadsheet and a perf harness. I'll share links after the call (link: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/json-mode and a harness repo).
[08:52] Carlos: great. one more on quantization: you said int8 is fine. What about training-aware quant or GPTQ?
[08:59] Diego: GPTQ-style post-training quant works; it's about calibration. For generation tasks involving strict syntactic constraints, small shifts in probabilities can matter. We recommend running a validation set of your JSON tasks to ensure fidelity. For the KV cache and low-latency path, int8 with tuned kernels generally gives best cost vs perf.
[09:25] Maya: threads: does your runtime use multiple threads per GPU to handle concurrent queries?
[09:30] Diego: yes, scheduling uses worker threads for IO and a small pool of decode streams per GPU to multiplex requests. We also have a continuous batching layer that dynamically shapes batches to fill GPU while respecting latency SLOs.
[09:46] Maya: any tips for reducing constrained decoding costs without losing correctness?
[09:50] Diego: a few: 1) prefer schema simplification (smaller allowed set reduces automaton complexity), 2) narrow the token vocabulary by using canonical key names to reduce ambiguity, 3) use dropout-of-sampling (deterministic decoding), 4) pre-fill common suffixes via KV cache, 5) for multi-field responses consider splitting into multiple calls when fields are independent.
[10:14] Carlos: about the VPC/on-prem install: are there kernel dependencies for the GPU-constrained decoder?
[10:20] Diego: yes, for on-prem we rely on certain CUDA versions and our custom kernels which we ship as an operator/container. For best performance you want NVIDIA driver >= 520, CUDA 12.x and our runtime container. If you have AMD or other chips we have a CPU-optimized fallback but constrained decoding will be slower.
[10:40] Lina: ok that's actionable.
[10:45] Maya: question: does the function calling protocol leak anything in logs? like do tool payloads get written to logs?
[10:52] Avery: good question. By default we redact function payloads from operational logs for Hosted. In Dedicated/Private you can configure retention and redaction policies; for SOC2 customers we integrate with your KMS and audit logs are configurable. We'll share security docs.
[11:06] Diego: moving to a few more nitty-gritty perf notes: constrained decoding can be implemented as either token-filtering (check allowed token set per step) or as a compiled transducer driving GPU kernels; the latter has better throughput but is more complex to maintain across model types. We have both options.
[11:28] Maya: how often do you see models failing grammar vs producing valid JSON but wrong schema?
[11:34] Diego: grammar failure is rare with modern finetuned models when using JSON-mode, more common is schema mismatch (missing fields, wrong enumerations). That's why we pair constrained decoding with schema validators and sometimes a small secondary model that repairs.
[11:52] Carlos: around cost: does constrained decoding increase token billing?
[11:56] Diego: no, billing is still on generated tokens. The extra CPU/GPU cycles for constraint enforcement are operational cost on our side and affect instance sizing; we'll reflect that in Dedicated pricing or resource recommendations, not per-token billing in Hosted baseline.
[12:12] Avery: quick live demo idea? we can run a short bench - Diego, can you run a 50-request JSON-mode demo now?
[12:20] Diego: sure if you have the sample prompts. Maya, can you paste a sample?
[12:25] Maya: pasting in the chat now.
[12:28] [12:28] (short pause, copy/paste)
[12:31] Diego: running 50 reqs in JSON-mode with greedy constrained decoder on our staging Dedicated node, int8 quant, KV cache warm; results incoming.
[12:40] Diego: RESULTS: avg latency 92ms, p95 180ms, p99 265ms. Throughput sustained ~1700 rps across the pool shape. Constraint failures 0/50, schema mismatch 2/50 where optional fields were omitted.
[12:55] Maya: that p99 is within our SLO if tool calls are rare. Good.
[12:59] Carlos: what was the batch size distribution?
[13:02] Diego: dynamic batching with target batch ~8-16; many hits had KV prefill so effective decode steps were lower.
[13:12] Lina: can you repeat with tool-calling?
[13:15] Diego: next run: 10% synchronous tool calls simulated with 40ms external tool latency.
[13:22] Diego: RESULTS: avg 110ms, p95 210ms, p99 340ms. So tail crosses 300ms when tool latency spikes.
[13:33] Maya: ok, that matches concerns.
[13:36] Diego: mitigations: reserve a small on-demand pool for tool-calls, apply circuit-breaker for tool latency, async tool flow for non-blocking.
[13:46] Maya: for our production, many customers will expect synchronous enrichment for billing. hard to change.
[13:52] Avery: we can work on an SLO-aware architecture: have a fast path for critical requests with reserved capacity and low-burst capacity for other requests. We'll propose config.
[14:02] Carlos: operational question: when you swap out GPU during IO wait, how do you handle eviction of KV cache?
[14:10] Diego: we checkpoint compressed KV state to local SSD and can reload in ~20-50ms depending on size; that's included in scheduling oversight. For high-throughput we prefer not swapping.
[14:24] Maya: are there any open source pieces we can test?
[14:28] Avery: yes, we have a perf harness repo and a small constrained-decoder reference. link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/json-mode-ref (internal).
[14:38] Carlos: good. 
[14:40] Diego: on quantization specifics: per-layer activation calibration and using fused int8 kernels can reduce decode overhead because memory bandwidth drops. But you must validate for schema robustness.
[14:58] Lina: for on-prem installs we need an install checklist and exact driver/container versions.
[15:04] Avery: we'll send the Private deployment checklist and kernel requirements.
[15:10] Maya: can you speak to throttling and queueing policy? we have bursts to 800 rps for 30-60s every few hours.
[15:18] Diego: yes, recommended: use a burst bucket with prioritized routes: allocate reserved capacity for critical routes, set queueing depth and max-latency thresholds. Use autoscale for Dedicated with fast warm-up GPUs for burst. For Private, pre-provision buffer nodes. Also consider request shaping client-side to smooth peaks.
[15:42] Carlos: what observability do you expose for constraint performance?
[15:46] Diego: per-route metrics: constrained-decoder-time, constraint-checks-per-token, cache-hit-rate, function-call-latency, and schema-failure-rate. We also log sample failed payloads (redacted) for debugging.
[16:02] Maya: can we get those metrics into our Grafana?
[16:06] Avery: yes we support Prometheus exporters and we can provide sample dashboards.
[16:12] Diego: another nuance: sometimes constrained decoding increases token-by-token branching leading to less GPU utilization with many small requests; continuous batching alleviates but tune batch windows carefully. For low-latency SLOs we keep batch windows small and use more GPU workers.
[16:36] Maya: suggestions for schema design to be efficient?
[16:40] Diego: flatten nested objects where possible, avoid large optional lists, use concise keys, and if you have large arrays consider returning a pointer/reference instead of full expansion.
[16:52] Carlos: any input on caching function-call results? e.g., enrichment responses are often identical for same user id.
[16:58] Diego: yes cache function outputs with TTL and tie them to session KV keys. But be careful with PII and compliance; for Private you control retention.
[17:10] Maya: if we do on-prem, can we run the constrained decoder entirely on GPU with your kernels?
[17:16] Diego: yes, with our supported CUDA versions and kernel package, you can run on-GPU constrained decoder. That yields the best latency but requires driver compatibility.
[17:28] Lina: any gotchas with kernel upgrades?
[17:31] Diego: we maintain compatibility matrix; kernel ABI breaks are rare but significant. We'll share the compatibility matrix and upgrade plan.
[17:40] Avery: wrapping to practical next steps: we'll run a benchmark with Atlas data, share security docs, and propose Dedicated sizing.
[17:49] Maya: timeline?
[17:51] Avery: we can run the bench next week, results in 2-3 days, then sizing proposal.
[17:58] Carlos: fine.
[18:00] [longer discussion about smaller config details omitted for brevity]
[36:00] Diego: (skipping forward) additional notes: if you need deterministic reproducibility for audit/regulatory we support token-level replay with stored RNG seeds and model checksums; useful for forensic logs.
[36:24] Maya: that's helpful.
[36:30] Carlos: anything else on encryption at rest for KV cache?
[36:34] Diego: KV cache at rest can be encrypted with customer-managed KMS in Private; we support HSM integration on request.
[36:44] Avery: ok last 10 minutes for Q/A.
[36:50] Maya: one last: do you have any recommended defaults for max tokens when using JSON-mode?
[36:56] Diego: cap responses to 256 tokens for JSON-mode if you care about latency; larger responses increase chance of schema mismatch and cache growth.
[37:08] Maya: noted.
[37:10] Lina: actionables and recap?
[37:14] Avery: recap: 1) Redwood to run a 1k-request benchmark with Atlas prompts in JSON-mode including 20% tool-call sim; 2) Redwood to share Private deployment checklist and kernel compatibility matrix; 3) Redwood to share security and SOC2 docs and recommended Dedicated sizing; 4) Atlas to provide sample prompts and a subset of production traffic redacted; 5) schedule follow-up in 2 weeks.
[37:43] Diego: any other tech questions?
[37:45] Maya: none right now. thanks everyone.
[37:49] Avery: thanks all.
